title: Walkway Modifier Check
description: Place modifiers so every description attaches to the intended word or action.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Reviewed for one-best-answer grammar logic, contextual editing, close distractors, and specific feedback.

questions.prompt: Choose the best revision: “After inspecting the walkway, several loose tiles were reported by Mina.”

options.text: After inspecting the walkway, several loose tiles were reported by Mina.
options.whyWrong: The opening phrase illogically suggests that the tiles performed the inspection.

options.text: Several loose tiles, after inspecting the walkway, were reported by Mina.
options.whyWrong: This still makes the tiles appear to perform the inspection.

options.text: Mina reported, after inspecting, the walkway several loose tiles.
options.whyWrong: The word order is awkward and obscures what was inspected.

options.text: After inspecting the walkway, Mina reported several loose tiles.

explanation.whyCorrect: Mina is placed directly after the introductory phrase, so the sentence clearly identifies who inspected the walkway.
explanation.quickTip: After an introductory modifier, name the person or thing that actually performs the action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means that staff used the west entrance and no other entrance?

options.text: Only staff used the west entrance.
options.whyWrong: This means no one except staff used that entrance; it does not limit which entrance staff used.

options.text: Staff used only the west entrance.
Staff only used the west entrance.
options.whyWrong: In careful editing, placing 'only' before the verb can ambiguously limit the action rather than the object.

options.text: Staff used the west only entrance.
options.whyWrong: This incorrectly suggests the west entrance is the only entrance that exists.

explanation.whyCorrect: Placing 'only' directly before 'the west entrance' limits the object and gives the intended meaning.
explanation.quickTip: Put limiting words such as only as close as possible to the word or phrase they limit.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest revision: “The crew replaced the railing near the stairs that was rusted.”

options.text: The crew replaced the rusted railing near the stairs.
Near the stairs that was rusted, the crew replaced the railing.
options.whyWrong: This makes the stairs appear to be rusted and also creates an agreement problem.

options.text: The crew near the stairs replaced the railing that was rusted.
options.whyWrong: This shifts 'near the stairs' to describe the crew rather than the railing location.

options.text: The rusted crew replaced the railing near the stairs.
options.whyWrong: This absurdly makes 'rusted' describe the crew.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'Rusted' sits directly before 'railing,' the noun it describes, while 'near the stairs' clearly identifies the railing's location.
explanation.quickTip: Keep descriptive clauses beside the noun they modify.

questions.prompt: Which revision fixes the dangling modifier? “While walking to the entrance, the broken light was easy to notice.”

options.text: While walking to the entrance, the broken light was easy to notice.
options.whyWrong: The sentence suggests the broken light was walking.

options.text: The broken light was walking to the entrance and easy to notice.
options.whyWrong: This changes the meaning and creates an illogical subject.

options.text: While walking to the entrance, I easily noticed the broken light.
Walking to the entrance was the broken light that I noticed.
options.whyWrong: The sentence remains illogical and awkward.

explanation.whyCorrect: The subject 'I' is the person who was walking, so the opening phrase now has a logical target.
explanation.quickTip: Ask who is doing the action in the opening phrase; name that subject immediately after the comma.

options.text: The supervisor nearly reviewed every report before noon.
options.whyWrong: This can mean the supervisor almost reviewed them but did not actually do so.

options.text: Nearly the supervisor reviewed every report before noon.
options.whyWrong: 'Nearly' is placed where it cannot logically modify the intended quantity.

options.text: The supervisor reviewed every nearly report before noon.
options.whyWrong: The modifier is in an ungrammatical position.

options.text: The supervisor reviewed nearly every report before noon.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'Nearly' directly modifies 'every report,' showing that most but not all reports were reviewed.
explanation.quickTip: Place degree and limiting modifiers beside the quantity or action they actually limit.

questions.prompt: Which revision makes the intended meaning clearest? “We saw a damaged sign beside the loading dock with a flashlight.”

options.text: With a flashlight, we saw a damaged sign beside the loading dock.
We saw with a damaged sign a loading dock beside the flashlight.
options.whyWrong: The revision destroys the intended relationships among the details.

options.text: We saw a damaged sign with a flashlight beside the loading dock.
options.whyWrong: This can make it sound as though the sign had the flashlight.

options.text: Beside the flashlight, the loading dock saw a damaged sign.
options.whyWrong: The loading dock cannot perform the action of seeing.

explanation.whyCorrect: Moving 'with a flashlight' to the beginning clearly shows how 'we' saw the sign.
explanation.quickTip: When a phrase could attach to two nouns, move it next to the word or action it truly describes.

questions.prompt: Choose the best revision: “Covered in rainwater, the custodian placed a warning cone beside the puddle.”

options.text: Covered in rainwater, the custodian placed a warning cone beside the puddle.
options.whyWrong: This says the custodian was covered in rainwater, which is not the intended meaning.

options.text: The custodian placed a warning cone beside the puddle that covered part of the walkway.
The puddle placed a warning cone beside the custodian.
options.whyWrong: This reverses the logical actor and action.

options.text: A warning cone, covered in rainwater, placed the custodian beside the puddle.
options.whyWrong: The cone cannot place the custodian.

explanation.whyCorrect: The descriptive clause now clearly explains that the puddle covered part of the walkway.
explanation.quickTip: Check that every descriptive phrase has a logical noun to modify.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids a misplaced modifier?

options.text: The team found a cracked tile during the inspection near the doorway.
options.whyWrong: 'Near the doorway' could attach to the inspection rather than clearly to the tile.

options.text: The cracked team found a tile near the doorway during the inspection.
options.whyWrong: 'Cracked' incorrectly modifies 'team'.

options.text: During the inspection, the team found a cracked tile near the doorway.
Near the doorway found the team a cracked tile.
options.whyWrong: The word order is not standard English.

explanation.whyCorrect: The time phrase is separated from the location phrase, making each modifier's job clear.
explanation.quickTip: Place time, location, and descriptive phrases where their targets are unmistakable.

curriculum.learningObjective: Place modifiers so every description attaches to the intended word or action.
